Look Who’s Coming to visit! In one month we have
Mark Gardner visiting for both a Saturday Demo
and follow-up classes. The month following we
have Craig Timmerman visiting. Both these gentlemen will be showing us creative methods to explore. Please read the article within to see WHY you
should make time for these events.
I've lost count of the number demos I have
watched regarding sharpening and lo and behold I
learn something new, or adapt my methods, almost
every time. Last meeting’s demo by Ed Pretty, stepping in for the ailing Dan Breck, was another nugget
learned! Thanks Ed for always being there for the
Guild!
In closing, I have a different type of President’s
Challenge for you. See what you can do to become
involved in Guild activities. Have a look around,
keep your ears peeled, and step up if you see someone needs help. Things you can do: Offer up some
spare wood for classes; offer to help harvest class
wood; take the easy Demonstrator Accreditation so
that you can do lathe demos for the club; sponsor
and lead a Guild exhibition or demonstration to the
public; hold a “sawdust huddle”, the list goes on.
Steve

On Saturday April 26, Mark will demonstrate two
innovative techniques that appeal to both the novice and experienced turner. For the follow-up classes one day will be spent on the hollowing and the
other on the shrink box. Sign-up for these classes
will start next week!!!
Turn hollow forms without the hollowing!
In this demo I'll show how I make hollow forms,
using green wood, much like you make lidded boxes only I'll glue the lid back on. Not only is there
less risk of turning through the side of your vessel
but it is also easier to gauge the wall thickness as
well as remove the shavings from the inside. I will
focus on techniques for making a precise joint to
help ensure that the piece stays together as it
dries. Time will be spent demonstrating various
ways to then hide the seam in your vessel. This vessel will also have handles.
Turn a shrink box.
A shrink box is a container that is made from green
wood with a bottom that is a dry disk of wood that
is fit into a groove in the base of the box. The
green wood box shrinks as it dries, locking the
bottom in place. Traditionally these were hand
carved. I’ll demonstrate how to turn the box, cut
the groove and carve and shape the bottom to
achieve a good tight fit. Typically turned wood
boxes are made from dry wood, I like this technique as it is a way to make lidded containers but
still use green wood.

In 2015 I attended a Betty Scarpino demonstration
and workshop hosted by the GVWG. https://
bettyscarpino.com/
I love the way her work can express so much with
simple curves and textures. After that demonstration I sketched an idea for a piece I would someday
like to make for my son and his wife. I took a carving course at Lee Valley Tools also in preparation
for making this piece. In 2024 the kids announced
the most wonderful news that they
were expecting a baby and I knew it
was time to get to work.
I began by turning one of my favourite woods, dogwood, into a disk.
But in order to capture the curve of
the smaller female figure I offset the
piece and recut it.
I didn’t have all the proper tools that Betty used
for this kind of work but
thought I could get by
with what I had. It
turned out to be a lot
more work than I anticipated doing the carving with my hand tools and
microcarver, files and LOTS of sanding.
(Continued on page 5)

I drilled a hole in the bottom of the sculpture and
one in the Guatambu base and glued a dowel between to hold up the piece.
In the end, I hope it conveys the love between the
couple and their unborn child and the love from
the hands that crafted it.
(Continued from page 4)

Why is a New Website Required?
The Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guild is
pleased to offer a preview of our new website and
member management system, marking a significant upgrade from our current platform.
The existing website and manual tracking of membership poses many challenges.
Our website is constructed with legacy technology.
Even the most straightforward task, like updating
the list of upcoming events, requires an in-depth
understanding of outdated technologies.
Additionally, the current website has no understanding of membership resulting in all content being publicly accessible. This limitation obstructs
member-to-member communication and prevents
an active community from developing. Currently
the Guild must directly email members to begin
every activity – even for something as simple as
letting other members know that there is wood
available.
Moreover, the absence of a comprehensive mass
emailing system compels Guild volunteers to create multiple batches of emails to circumvent SPAM
restrictions; while the lack of an integrated payment and member tracking system means that
membership and payment details are managed
across multiple spreadsheets.
What Does the New System Offer?
The new website and member management system provide numerous enhancements, including:
•
Public and Member-Only Areas: Ensuring enhanced privacy and the ability to foster member to member communications via forums and
special interest groups.
•
News of What’s Happening: Keeping members
abreast of the latest activities, including newsletter being available, significant member milestones, and other notices of significant happenings.
•
Calendar of Upcoming Events: Facilitating the
viewing, registration, and payment for classes
and special events online and with ease.
•
Online Membership Directory: Enabling members to find one another, while enabling members to control the information available or if
they appear. Member information is never
available to the public.
•
Special Interest Groups and Forums: Enabling
members to self organize Wood Cutting Parties,
Sawdust Huddles, and exchange ideas in Tech
Talk and Focus on Fundament forums.
•
Photo Albums: Providing a platform to share
pictures, including the ability to tag photos for
inclusion in each months Instant Gallery and
President’s Challenge.
•
And many other resources designed to enhance
the member experience and simplify the management and day-to-day functions of the Guild.
When is This Happening?
The new website is currently undergoing testing
and will be formally introduced with a brief presentation at the April meeting. The official launch is
anticipated shortly thereafter.
Can I See Anything Now?
Yes, a preview of the public area of the new website is available at gvwg.clubexpress.com.

Our Guild has a reputation throughout the AAW for
inviting quality turners to demonstrate and teach
classes here. We usually bring in 3-4 per year. To
make this work we need at least 40 members to
attend the Saturday Demo and we need to fill the
class, or classes, that follow. But, without that level
of participation we lose money and, in the long
term, we cannot sustain this important part of our
Guild activity.
Here are some of the reasons I have heard from
members not attending these events:
•
Scheduling Conflict – yet the Guild schedules
these things months – even years in advance.
Of course, things come up in our busy lives but
with so much lead time we can at least pencil it
in to our calendars.
•
Cost – at $35 for the whole day it is cheaper
than a pretty piece of wood or a new tool and is
certainly cheaper than traveling anywhere to
see similar events.
•
I am not good enough – If you are a new turner
these sessions are where you need to be. These
demonstrators are EXCELLENT teachers. Every
demonstrator offers a wealth of “tips”, “tricks”,
“nuggets”, “gems”, “tools”, or whatever you
want to call them. And they are all there for the
taking. And you get to discuss them with the
demonstrator at lunch or during breaks.
•
I am not interested in what s/he does – regardless of what they are doing it is still turning and
elements of it are usable in all areas of turning.
A few testimonials…
“I have attended most of the over 100 sessions we
have held and can say that I have gathered something
useful from every one of them. I have also traveled
to 11 AAW symposiums and can attest that our intimate day-long sessions are every bit as valuable as
a 3-day symposium with over sixty 90-minute
demonstrations. For me these demonstrations are
incredibly useful and I challenge each member to
try it just once. After that I am sure you will be
hooked.” – Bruce Campbell
“What can you buy for $35.00? How about an idea,
a relationship, a meaningful conversation, a unique
experience, a new challenge, a better skill set, and
a moment doing something just for yourself. For all
of us, sharp can be sharper, an exceptional person
can be inspiring, communication improves any situation, new ideas can be stimulating, everyone can
learn to dance and wood turners are fun to be with.
My tools are now sharper in several ways after
attending Eric Lofstrom’s all-day demonstration at
Sapperton Pensioners Hall on Nov 12th. To begin
with Eric is having a wonderful life and he shared
that with us. My tool presentation has improved
because of his hints. I am now aware that turning
requires all moving body parts and I met two new
delightful people at the demo. Not bad for thirty
five bucks. Do something for yourself while supporting your Guild. Open up to something that will
be good for you. Consider coming to the next
presentation, you will leave with much more than
(Continued on page 8)

Page 8
what is in the topic description.” -Dave Urquhart
“Eric, as always, was an enthusiastic presenter. I
find it unfortunate that so many members missed
this particular demonstration, especially new and
intermediate turners. I know that many turners
have difficulty with tool control because of the
questions that I hear being asked. Eric’s presentation was so easy to understand that I know every
one of us at the presentation took away skills that
will change how we turn without having to buy a
single new tool. For less than the price of the
cheapest accessory every member could have been
able to increase their skill level significantly. Eric’s
presentation of biomechanics as it relates to
woodturning was both an affirmation of what I already understand and an extension of that same
understanding. I use the horizontal movements
that he demonstrated but my vertical movements
up until now have been controlled arm movements.
I can now see that the level of control that I have
for horizontal movements can now be extended
vertical movements as well. This will give me greater three-dimensional control. I’m still a little edgy
about removing my anti fatigue mat but I understand his logic, so will give it a try - but probably
not with bare feet. The take-aways for me were
many but the foremost of all was the skew with the
convex bevel. Just the concept of using a convex
bevel rocked my little woodturning world. Our conventional thinking for what seems like forever has
been that a bevel must be concave or at least flat
to be able to control the cut. Even though this flew
in the face of everything that I have understood, he
was still able to make it possible for me to understand the advantage of not allowing chips to get
into the gap created by the typical concave grind of
the bevel. I’ve accepted the fact that chips get between the tool and the work on heavy cuts but it
never occurred to me that the problem still existed
when making fine cuts and often wondered why I
would get little “divots” in an otherwise clean cut. I
will definitely be modifying a skew with a convex
bevel. It seems to me the round -edged skew used
by the well-known Moroccan turner in the bazaar
must have a convex bevel since it’s the only tool he
uses for all cuts, including tight coves.” - Ed Pretty

15% Discount for GVWG Members!
How to Qualify:
•Stop giving your phone number at the cashier
counter. (Will be hard because we have been
doing this for years).
•Only tell them you are with the GVWG or Greater
Vancouver Woodturners Guild.
•Either statement will link your purchase to your
new 15% discount.
If you give the cashier your phone number, you will
only get the store 5% non-guild price.
By saying GVWG instead you get 15% guild price
If you are buying something that needs a warranty,
you just give them your Name and Address and that
will go on the electronic file.
If the item you are buying has a flyer sale that is
better than the 15%, then you will automatically get
the better price.
Every purchase you make in the store by doing the
above process adds to our GVWG Credit account.
We use this credit account to buy KMS Gift certificate prizes and even bought our Laguna lathe for
Sapperton Hall with this credit account. By doing
this you are giving yourself a better discount and
helping the guild at the same time.
If you are an out of town guild member, all you
have to do is type in GVWG as the customer name
when buying, and type in your full name, address
etc. in the ship to and you will get the 15% discount.
The 15% is an average savings and is based on the
cost margins from that manufacturer. This does not
apply to published special flyer items.
If we all do this, we can even get up to a bigger discount level in future!

Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild

The guild is looking to build up its pool of Instructors for the Introduction to Turning program
(formerly know as Turning 101). In recent years our
pool has been cut in half, limiting the number of
classes we can offer each year. We are thankful
that Claudia Hayward & Ed Pretty have continued
to lead classes however the demand is greater than
two people can support.
What is Introduction to Turning and what is
the time commitment?
Introduction to Turning is actually two separate
classes focused on introducing new turners to the
basics of either bowl turning or spindle turning.
Intro to Bowl Turning is delivered over 3 days (One
weekend and the following Saturday), while Intro
to Spindle turning is a 2-day course (One weekend).
The Guild’s goal is to deliver both classes at least
twice per year, once in the Fall (September to November) and again in Winter / Spring (February to
April).
We are looking to build up a pool of Instructors
willing to teach one class in either the Fall or Winter / Spring seasons, so the time commitment
would be 2 or 3 days per year depending upon the
course taught.
What are the Benefits?
This is a voluntary rather than paid role. While
there is no monetary compensation, Ed and Claudia point to many personal benefits that they have
experienced through instructing, in particular
•
Enjoyment and satisfaction from helping others
learn and overcome barriers
•
Personal fulfilment from giving back, passing on
knowledge and sharing their passion
•
Becoming a better turner though developing a
deeper understanding of woodturning practices
They attest, “When you have to explain and
demonstrate ideas and principles to others in a
simple way, you gain awareness and insight that
you would otherwise take for granted, and you become a better turner.”
Do you have the Right Stuff?
The Guild is looking for experienced turners who
are proficient in either bowl or spindle turning or
both. Prospective Instructors must have the Guild’s
Demonstrator certification and the following competencies:
1) Woodturning Knowledge
A comprehensive understanding of woodturning
fundamentals, in particular safe turning practices.
2) Woodturning Competency
Proficiency with key bowl turning cuts including
push & shear cuts, shear scraping, negative rake
scraping and forming a tenon.
and / or
Proficiency with key spindle turning cuts, particularly the skew, forming beads with both a skew &
spindle gouge, and forming coves with a spindle
gouge.
(Continued on page 10)

March 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 10
3) Teaching Competency
A structured approach to delivering content and
following a lesson plan, including
•
Time management / pacing a class
•
Reading participants and adapting to their
learning styles
•
Provide feedback in a constructive / nonthreatening manner
•
Establish 2-way communication with participants rather than 1-way "lecture"
•
Observation and assessment - recognize incorrect technique and provide guidance on how to
correct
The Guild can help prospective Instructors develop
their teaching competencies though mentoring,
including a one day “in shop” train the trainer session to walk though each phase of the Intro to
Bowl or Spindle turning classes and workshop common issues and challenges.
In addition, the Guild is currently documenting
standardized lesson plans for each class that new
Instructors will be able to use a blueprint for delivering their own classes.
Are you interest in joining the team?
If are interested in learning more about becoming
an Intro to Training Instructor, please email Peter
Hill at peterhill64@telus.net . Ideally, we would like
to have at least 1 additional Bowl and Spindle turning instructor in place for the Fall season and
would be looking to develop those instructors over
the summer.
(Continued from page 9)
Last month, we held our first Intro to Turning Bowls
course of the year! Over two weekends, our five
eager participants learned about the basics of bowl
turning from lead instructor Claudia Hayward with
assistance from Matt Lo and Keith Ruttan. On the
first day, everyone came into the KMS classroom
with various levels of experience, from those who
had never done woodworking before, to those that
had been experimenting on the lathe for a few
years. Over the three days, everyone was taught
about safety, proper turning technique and the
bowl turning process then allowed to practice as
much as possible on green wood blanks. Hundreds
of push cuts were made and tools traveled many
kilometers over the students’ work, resulting in
piles of shavings and a great time had by all. On the
last day, the benefits of focused practice were evident as everyone was turning with more confidence and better technique than when the class
began. Of course, Intro to Turning is only a starting
point, so please support and encourage these
green turners as they progress on their woodturning journeys.
Special thanks to Michael Moult and Simon Britchford who provided all of the green turning blanks
for this course. An extra special thank-you to Brian
Lunt who helps make these classes possible by
handling classroom booking with KMS, letting us in
on class days and supporting the instructors
throughout the days.

 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 24)

March 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 24
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage and GVWG Safety
webpage.
(Continued from page 23)
